Instead, she moved the stones higher and said he was changing his ____2____. I wanted her first snowman to ____3____.

The next morning, he leaned to one side. We added a scarf, which made the lean look almost ____4____. My sister asked me to take a photograph. I chose an angle that hid the uneven body. She wanted to remember the way he looked ____5____, not the way he had looked yesterday. My attempt to make a better picture had removed the very ____6____ she found funny.

By afternoon, the carrot lay on the ground. My sister collected it and returned the stones to the garden edge. I offered to find more snow in a shaded corner, but she shook her head. "We can make another one when it snows again," she said. That was a ____7____, not a demand that this one stay forever. I had treated the melting as a problem to ____8____. She was already thinking about the next ____9____.

We printed two photographs: the round snowman and the leaning one. She put them beside a drawing of the gate in summer. The pictures did not tell a story in which one season had ____10____ another. They showed different things she liked about the same place. I began to understand why she had not wanted my careful ____11____. It made a tidier snowman but a less ____12____ memory.

Later, I found a smile stone and returned it to the garden. The snowman had gone, but the afternoon was not ____13____. Photographs and stories remained. My sister enjoyed a brief thing without demanding that it become ____14____. Next time it snows, I will help roll the first ball and leave the ____15____ to her.
